scLimbsCoveredByACT: Limb (trigger): 'If keyboard focus CAN BE MOVED TO a component using a keyboard interface' — covered by every applicable case using natively focusable <a>/<button>, plus the focusability boundary tested via tabindex (Passed 2: div tabindex=1; Passed 3: div tabindex=-1).

Limb (core, PASS): 'focus CAN BE MOVED AWAY from that component using only a keyboard interface' with standard Tab/Shift-Tab — Passed 1 (96eb4b: link+button, trivially no trap) and Passed 7 (d2f5325: onblur redirect that still lets focus resolve forward/back).

Limb (core, FAIL): focus CANNOT be moved away — the hard keyboard trap. Failed 1 (f5ea9fd: button onblur refocuses itself) and Failed 2 (0ec0e93: two self-refocusing buttons). These are the only true 'stuck on one element' traps.

Limb (conditional pass): 'if it requires MORE THAN unmodified arrow or tab keys or other standard exit methods, the user IS ADVISED of the method for moving focus away' — covered on the PASS side three ways: advice text BEFORE the trap (Passed 4: 'Press Ctrl+M to Exit' precedes buttons), advice text amid/within the trap (Passed 5), and advice revealed via a keyboard-accessible help link inside the subset (Passed 6: showHelpText). These map to G21's documented-escape mechanisms and Understanding's puzzle-applet/WYSIWYG examples.

Limb (conditional pass FAILURE modes): the 'user is advised' clause violated three distinct ways on the FAIL side — custom exit (Ctrl+M) exists but is NEVER advised (Failed 3: 7dcc4ae); advice present but is generic/non-instructive and does not describe the method (Failed 4: 8fba391 'Go to the next element'); advice present and names the correct key BUT the custom exit does not actually work (Failed 5: 62fd24e — text says Ctrl+M but the onkeydown escape handler is removed). Failed 5 directly exercises Trusted Tester Evaluate-Results step 1.b / How-to-Test 3.b ('determine whether the alternate command(s) work').

Limb (scope/applicability — DNA): 'Not applicable if the page has no components that can receive keyboard focus' (TT DNA; EN 'does not contain relevant content') — covered four ways: no focusable content at all (Inapplicable 1: only <h1>), disabled control (Inapplicable 2: button disabled), display:none (Inapplicable 3), and visibility:hidden (Inapplicable 4). Good coverage of the non-focusable boundary.
scLimbsAbsentFromACT: The ENTIRE multi-format / plug-in / embedded-application trap class — the central scenario in the Understanding 'Intent' ('common problem when multiple formats are combined within a page and rendered using plug-ins or embedded applications') and the ONLY mapped Failure technique F10 ('combining multiple content formats in a way that traps users inside one format type'; example: tabbing into a plug-in and being unable to return). Zero cases contain an <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, applet, or any cross-format/cross-document boundary. The corpus simulates ALL traps with inline JS onblur/onkeydown on plain HTML buttons.

Modal dialog / popover intentional focus restriction — Understanding explicitly carves this out ('appropriate for a web page to restrict focus to a subsection... when the user is inside a modal dialog or popover... does not fail... as long as the user knows how to untrap') and gives a full modal example (Cancel/OK/Esc, focus cycles within dialog). TT Test 4.C Note 2.b says focus SHOULD remain within a modal until closed but you must check for traps WITHIN it. No case uses role=dialog, aria-modal, a popover, or any focus-cycling-within-a-container construct.

The Esc key as a 'standard exit method' — Understanding singles out Esc as 'a commonly used standard exit method.' Every scripted custom-exit case uses Ctrl+M; no case tests Esc (nor any platform 'standard exit method' beyond Tab) as the untrap mechanism.

Arrow-key navigation/traps — the SC text and TT both name 'unmodified arrow keys' as standard navigation and a potential trap surface (composite/grid/menu widgets). No case uses arrow-key handling, roving tabindex, or any arrow-driven component (menus, grids, listboxes, sliders, tab panels, radio groups).

The page-section 'loop' trap distinct from a single-element trap — TT 2.b: 'keyboard access is restricted to a small section of the page with no way to navigate out of the loop to the rest of the page.' The corpus's traps are single-element self-refocus (Failed 1/2) or 2-button ping-pong loops with a documented exit; there is no genuine MULTI-element region/landmark loop that walls off the rest of a substantive page.

The TT exception 'a section that requires input/interaction before allowing focus to progress is NOT a failure' (e.g., a required field or step gating progress) — no required-form-field / sequential-gate scenario exists (no <form>, <input>, <select>, or <textarea> anywhere in the SC's corpus).

Real ARIA/custom-widget traps with author-implemented keyboard handling (the Understanding 'custom components and widgets not implemented with keyboard users in mind') — e.g., a date-picker/calendar widget (one of the Understanding examples), rich-text/WYSIWYG editor (another example, with Alt+F10 exit), carousel, or autocomplete. None present; all controls are bare native <a>/<button>.

Conformance Requirement 5 / Non-Interference framing — F10's title and TT baseline tie 2.1.2 to CR5 (a trap on one part interferes with the whole page). No case frames the trap as blocking access to OTHER conformant content downstream; pages are too small (1-7 controls) to exhibit interference at page scale.

Advice-timing nuance: G21 requires escape instructions to PRECEDE entering the sub-content (or be reachable within it via keyboard). Only Passed 4 places advice before; Passed 5/6 place it within. No FAIL case isolates the failure of 'instructions exist but appear only AFTER/downstream of the trap so a keyboard user cannot reach them' as a distinct timing/reachability defect.
contentDomainsPresent: Plain HTML text/links (anchor <a href='#'> + <button>) with no styling
Non-interactive elements made focusable via tabindex (div tabindex=1 positive; div tabindex=-1 programmatic-only)
Inline-JavaScript event-handler traps: onblur self-refocus (setTimeout focus loops) and onfocus/onblur/onkeydown handlers driving focus between elements
Scripted custom-key escape mechanism (shared keyboard.js: Ctrl+M handler, trapOn flag, moveFocusToButton/moveFocusTo, showHelpText)

Textual exit instructions as static

('Press Ctrl+M to Exit') and as JS-revealed help text via a help link
Non-focusable / hidden states for inapplicability: bare <h1>, disabled attribute, display:none, visibility:hidden
varietyGaps: Content technology is a monoculture: 16/16 cases are tiny single-purpose HTML stubs (max 7 controls, no CSS, no real page chrome) built ONLY from <a>, <button>, and <div tabindex>. The only 'mechanism' for trapping is inline JS onblur/onkeydown. There is no diversity of trap MECHANISM — the canonical real-world traps (plug-in/embedded-app/iframe per F10 and the Intent, and ARIA widget keyboard-handling bugs) are entirely simulated-away.

No iframe / object / embed / cross-format boundary at all — this is the single biggest gap because it is exactly what the SC's Intent and its only Failure technique (F10) describe; a checker/LLM trained on this corpus would never see a true plug-in/iframe trap.

No modal-dialog or popover scenarios — so the permitted-restriction carve-out (focus intentionally trapped in a dialog with an Esc/standard untrap) and the 'trap-WITHIN-a-modal' sub-check (TT Note 2.b) are completely untested. This is a high-value gap given modals are the most common modern focus-trap pattern.

Exit-key monoculture: custom exit is always Ctrl+M; the Esc key (explicitly named in Understanding as the prototypical 'standard exit method') and arrow-key exits/navigation are never exercised. No roving-tabindex / arrow-driven widget (menu, grid, listbox, slider, tablist, radiogroup).

No real 'section loop' / region-scoped trap distinct from single-element self-refocus, and no Non-Interference (CR5) framing where a trap blocks access to substantial downstream page content — pages are too small to show page-scale interference.

Form/input domain entirely missing: no <form>, <input>, <select>, <textarea>, contenteditable, required-field gating, or autocomplete — so the TT 'required interaction before progressing is not a failure' exception and editor/WYSIWYG examples have no representation.

Advice-quality FAIL coverage is good (undocumented exit, wrong/generic text, non-working command) but advice-TIMING/REACHABILITY is undertested: no FAIL where the only instructions sit downstream of the trap and are therefore unreachable by keyboard (the precise defect G21 guards against).

Outcome balance is shallow on the PASS side's most important real category: of 7 passes, 4 are trivial-no-trap/focusability checks and only 3 exercise the 'advised custom-exit' limb; combined with 0 in-scope ACT rules, automated coverage of 2.1.2 is effectively nil and the corpus leans on artificial JS stubs rather than authentic component traps.

aspects.title: F10 cross-format / embedded-application trap (iframe, object, embed, plug-in, shadow-DOM widget) — the SC's central and only mapped failure technique
aspects.description: F10 is the single failure technique mapped to 2.1.2 and it describes the SC's archetypal scenario: keyboard focus enters embedded or cross-format content and cannot be moved back out to the host document. Every ACT case simulates traps with inline JS onblur/onkeydown on bare native <button>s in one document; ZERO cases contain an <iframe>, <object>, <embed>, applet, web-component/Shadow-DOM widget, or any document/format boundary. The human-judgment surface: deciding whether focus that has entered an embedded boundary can return to the parent, whether the embedded content provides an exit, and whether any escape advice is present, keyboard-reachable, and accurate across a boundary the page author may not control. This is exactly the F10 intent the corpus never exercises.
aspects.scLimb: Core limb (FAIL): focus CANNOT be moved away — applied to the cross-format/embedded boundary that the SC Intent calls its archetypal cause and that F10 (the only mapped failure) describes.
aspects.whyUncovered: All ACT cases use plain inline-scripted native buttons in a single document; none contains an iframe, object, embed, applet, web-component/Shadow-DOM widget, or any cross-format boundary, so the corpus never exercises F10 at all despite F10 being the only failure technique listed for the SC. A static checker cannot drive focus across an iframe/shadow boundary and observe whether the next Tab returns to the parent.

references.quote: Some plug-ins create a common situation in which the keyboard focus can become "stuck" in a plug-in, leaving a keyboard-only user with no way to return to the other content.
A user tabs into a plug-in and is unable to return to content outside the plug-in content with the keyboard.
This is a common problem when multiple formats are combined within a page and rendered using plug-ins or embedded applications
If the plug-in does not provide a keyboard mechanism to return focus to the parent window, users who must use the keyboard may become trapped in the plug-in content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages that introduce a real focus boundary using <iframe srcdoc="...">, custom elements with attachShadow({mode:'open', delegatesFocus:true}), or <object>/<svg> with focusable children. Inside the boundary, wire onblur self-refocus or a Tab handler that loops back to the boundary's first control so Tab never crosses back to a parent-document <a> link that follows. For PASS variants, let the final Tab cross the boundary OR provide a working, keyboard-reachable Esc/documented exit inside the boundary. The trap must be invisible in light-DOM source so static markup inspection cannot resolve it. Place a clearly-labeled 'AFTER' link after the embed so the judge can confirm whether forward Tab ever reaches it.
suggestedScenarios: An <iframe srcdoc> whose inner document has a button that calls focus() on itself onblur, so Tab inside the iframe never returns focus to the parent document's following <a> link; no exit advice anywhere (FAIL).

An <iframe> embedding a tiny editor whose last focusable control loops Tab back to its own first control so Tab never crosses the iframe boundary back to the parent, with NO instructions about how to leave it (FAIL).

A custom web component using Shadow DOM (delegatesFocus) that re-grabs focus onblur, trapping Tab inside the shadow tree; the host page provides no documented escape and the trap is invisible in the light-DOM source (FAIL).

The same Shadow-DOM widget but WITH a visible instruction inside the shadow root saying 'Press Escape to leave editor' AND a working Esc handler that blurs the active element — a genuine PASS a tool cannot confirm because it must drive Esc through the shadow boundary.

An <object> embedding inline SVG with focusable <a> elements whose script keeps focus inside the SVG; a paragraph BEFORE the object reads 'Tab through the diagram, then Tab again to continue' — but Tab in fact loops, so the advice is present yet false (F10 fail masked by plausible text).

An <iframe> media-controls panel where Tab cycles play/pause/seek and correctly exits to the parent after the last control (true PASS per G21 mechanism #1) — a human must Tab to the final control and confirm the next Tab crosses the boundary.

aspects.title: Modal-dialog / popover focus restriction: legitimate containment vs. an undismissable trap (the Understanding carve-out)
aspects.description: The Understanding explicitly states that intentional focus restriction inside a modal dialog or popover does NOT fail the SC, AS LONG AS the user knows how to untrap and leave. Trusted Tester Test 4.C reinforces this: focus SHOULD remain within a modal until it is closed, but you must check for traps WITHIN it. This poses a pure human-judgment question the corpus never asks: is a focus-cycling dialog a CONFORMANT modal (a discoverable, keyboard-operable dismiss — Esc, or a reachable Cancel/Close button) or a TRAP (no keyboard-reachable way to close, a non-functional close, or a focus cycle that EXCLUDES the close control)? Distinguishing the two requires understanding the dialog's intent and confirming the dismiss path actually works — semantic and behavioral judgment a tool cannot make. No corpus case uses role=dialog, aria-modal, <dialog>, popover, or any focus-cycling container.
aspects.scLimb: Conditional-pass / carve-out limb: intentional focus restriction in a modal/popover does NOT fail PROVIDED the user can untrap and leave — distinguishing conformant containment from an undismissable trap.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains no dialog/popover construct of any kind; its only focus-cycling cases (Failed 1/2 self-refocus, the 2-button ping-pong) are framed as unconditional traps, never as the legitimate-modal carve-out, so the conformant-containment-vs-trap distinction is never tested. A checker can detect a focus cycle but cannot judge whether the cycle includes a working keyboard-operable dismiss.

references.quote: There may be times when it's appropriate for a web page to restrict focus to a subsection of the content – for example, when the user is inside a modal dialog or popover. This does not fail the requirements of this criterion, as long as the user knows how to "untrap" the focus and leave that component.
The dialog is dismissed by activating the "Cancel" button, the "OK" button, or the Esc key.
Keyboard focus **should remain within a modal dialog box** until it is closed (per Test 4.F Step 3); however, check for keyboard traps **within** the dialog.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build dialogs with role=dialog/aria-modal or native <dialog open>, plus popovers via the popover attribute, that cycle Tab among their controls. Vary the SINGLE variable that decides conformance: presence/absence of a keyboard-reachable dismiss. Conformant PASS = wrap cycle includes a focusable Close + working Esc handler. Traps = no Close and no Esc handler; OR Close exists but is excluded from the Tab cycle; OR Close is mouse-only (onclick, not focusable, no keydown); OR advice 'Press Esc to dismiss' present but no Esc listener wired. Keep visual appearance identical between conformant and trap variants so only keyboard-driving resolves them.
suggestedScenarios: A <dialog open> modal that traps Tab cycling among its controls but has NO close/cancel button and NO Esc handler — a genuine trap masquerading as an ordinary modal (FAIL).
A conformant role=dialog whose Tab cycle wraps last-to-first AND includes a keyboard-operable 'Close' button plus a working Esc handler — a PASS the corpus never models.
A modal whose only dismiss is an X icon that responds to onclick (mouse) but is not focusable and has no keydown handler — closeable by mouse, trapped by keyboard (FAIL).
A modal that HAS a focusable 'Close' button, but the focus-trap script excludes it from the Tab cycle (cycles only the form fields), so the user can see Close but can never Tab to it (FAIL).
A popover (popover attribute) that grabs focus on open and re-focuses its first element onblur, with text 'Press Esc to dismiss' but NO Esc listener wired, so the documented exit is false (FAIL).

Two stacked modals where Esc on the top returns focus to the underlying modal correctly (PASS) vs. a variant where Esc closes the top but drops focus to <body> and Tab restarts the trap (FAIL) — distinguishing graceful nested-dismiss from a re-trap.

aspects.title: Esc and other platform 'standard exit methods' as the untrap mechanism — and whether they actually fire
aspects.description: The Understanding names Esc as a commonly-used standard exit method and notes other platform-specific standard methods may exist; crucially, if focus can be moved away using a STANDARD exit method, NO advice is required — the advice clause only triggers for non-standard methods. Every scripted custom-exit case in the corpus uses Ctrl+M, a non-standard combo that always requires advice. The corpus therefore never tests the judgment call of whether a given key counts as a standard exit method (so no advice is owed), nor whether an Esc-based exit actually works. A human must (a) decide a key qualifies as standard for the platform and (b) verify pressing it genuinely releases focus — behavior a tool cannot evaluate and which the spec deliberately leaves to author/auditor interpretation. This is a false-positive trap: a checker seeing a focus cycle with no advice text would wrongly flag a page that passes because Esc releases focus.
aspects.scLimb: Boundary of the conditional-pass clause: when the exit uses a 'standard exit method' (Esc/arrows/Tab), NO advice is owed — versus a non-standard method that requires advice; and whether the named exit key actually fires.
aspects.whyUncovered: No corpus case uses Esc (or any platform standard exit beyond Tab/Shift-Tab) as the release mechanism; all scripted exits are Ctrl+M, collapsing the standard-vs-non-standard distinction. The spec leaves 'standard exit method' to human interpretation, and verifying that Esc actually releases focus requires driving the keyboard — neither is automatable.

references.quote: Generally, in most environments with a physical keyboard, pressing the Esc key is a commonly used "standard exit method", but other platform-specific methods may be available.

This specification does not define what constitutes a "standard exit method" – this is dependent on the user's hardware, user agent, and operating system, and as such will require some interpretation from authors and auditors.

If untrapping focus requires a different method (rather than unmodified arrow keys, the Tab key, or other "standard exit methods"), content can still pass this criterion provided that the user is advised how they can untrap focus using their keyboard interface.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build focus-cycling widgets whose ONLY release mechanism is Esc (or another arguably-standard key) and deliberately omit advice text — these are PASSes that a naive checker flags. Contrast with widgets that preventDefault() Esc (so it does nothing) and only release on Ctrl+M with no advice (FAIL). Add a Failed-5-style defect on the standard-key axis: advice says 'Press Esc to leave' but the handler checks the wrong keyCode. Include a platform-specific variant (Alt+F10 / Option+F10 from the WYSIWYG example) to exercise the author/auditor interpretation of what counts as 'standard'. Test exit from EACH focus position, not just one — a widget may swallow Esc only for some controls.
suggestedScenarios: A focus-cycling widget that releases focus to the page on Esc with NO advice text — a PASS (Esc is a standard exit method, no advice owed) that a checker would wrongly flag as 'trap with no documented exit'.

A widget where the script preventDefault()s Esc (Esc does nothing) while only Ctrl+M escapes, with no advice — a FAIL, directly contrastable with the case above; distinguishing requires actually pressing Esc.

A trap whose documented exit is 'Press Esc to leave' but the keydown handler checks keyCode 13 (Enter) by mistake, so Esc never fires — advice names a standard key yet the implementation is wrong (FAIL).

A WYSIWYG-style editor that releases focus on the platform-specific Alt+F10 / Option+F10 WITH appropriate advice (PASS) vs. the same without advice — testing whether Alt+F10 is 'standard' enough to need or not need advice.

A modal where both Esc and Cancel release focus, but a script swallows Esc only when a child <input> is focused — Esc works from some controls and silently fails from others; a human must test exit from EACH focus position.
A widget that releases focus on arrow keys (unmodified, explicitly named as standard) with no advice — PASS — vs. one that releases only on a non-standard combo with no advice — FAIL.

aspects.title: Arrow-key / roving-tabindex composite-widget traps (menu, grid, listbox, radiogroup, tablist, slider)
aspects.description: The SC text and Trusted Tester both name unmodified arrow keys as standard navigation, and the Understanding's calendar-widget example is built on arrow navigation. Composite widgets implemented with roving tabindex commonly capture arrow keys inside the widget; the conformance question is whether Tab/Shift-Tab still moves focus OUT of the widget even when arrows are captured. The corpus contains NO arrow-driven widget at all — it only tests Tab/Shift-Tab on flat lists of buttons. The judgment a human must make is semantic: recognize the construct as a composite widget, understand its expected interaction model (arrows move within, Tab moves out), and confirm Tab is not also swallowed. A roving-tabindex widget that also intercepts Tab is a trap; one that lets Tab pass is fine — a distinction tools cannot draw without driving both arrow and Tab keys and understanding widget semantics.
aspects.scLimb: Core limb applied to the standard-arrow-navigation surface the SC explicitly names: focus can be moved away via Tab even when arrow keys are captured by a composite widget — versus a widget that also swallows Tab.
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero corpus cases use arrow-key handling, roving tabindex, or any composite-widget role (menu/grid/listbox/radiogroup/tablist/slider); the corpus never tests the standard arrow-navigation surface the SC explicitly calls out. Determining whether arrows-captured-but-Tab-exits is a pass requires driving both key classes and understanding the widget's intended model — not automatable.

references.quote: Keyboard focus is not considered trapped when the user can navigate away from a component using only a keyboard interface, and if it only requires unmodified arrow or Tab keys or other "standard exit methods".

A calendar widget allows users to add, remove or update items in their calendar using the keyboard. The controls in the widget are part of the tab order within the web page, allowing users to tab through the controls in the widget as well as to any links or controls that follow.
Use **standard navigation keys** (e.g., TAB, SHIFT+TAB, arrow keys, CTRL+TAB, etc.) to navigate through all keyboard focusable elements on the page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Implement composite widgets with roving tabindex (one element tabindex=0, others tabindex=-1) and arrow-key handlers that move focus among items. The conformance variable is the Tab handler: PASS = Tab/Shift-Tab left alone so focus exits to the next control (matching the Understanding calendar example); FAIL = the widget also preventDefault()s Tab so once focus enters there is no exit and no advice. Add a within-widget arrow loop variant (last item ArrowRight wraps to first AND Tab swallowed). Add a misleading-advice variant where Tab DOES exit but instructions say 'Use Tab to move between options' — not a strict failure if Tab still exits, testing whether the judge correctly rules exit works despite a wrong mental model. Always place an 'AFTER' control to confirm whether Tab reaches it.
suggestedScenarios: A role=menu with roving tabindex where arrows move among items and the script also preventDefault()s Tab, so once focus enters the menu there is no Tab exit and no documented alternative (FAIL).

A role=grid date picker where arrows move between day cells but BOTH Tab and Shift-Tab are captured to keep focus in the grid, with no instructions (FAIL) vs. the same grid where Tab correctly exits to the next control (PASS per the calendar example).

A role=tablist with arrow navigation among tabs where focusing a tab steals and retains focus (onblur refocus) so Tab can never reach the panel or beyond — a composite-widget version of the corpus's self-refocus trap (FAIL).
A custom <div role=slider> that captures ArrowUp/ArrowDown AND Tab ('to prevent accidental value loss'), trapping the user on the slider with no escape advice (FAIL).

A roving-tabindex toolbar where ArrowRight cycles buttons and at the last button focus wraps to the first instead of allowing exit, and Tab is also swallowed — a within-widget loop trap distinct from a single self-refocus (FAIL).

A listbox where arrows navigate options and Tab DOES exit, but instructions wrongly say 'Use Tab to move between options' — not a strict 2.1.2 failure since Tab still exits (PASS), testing whether the judge correctly rules exit works despite misleading advice.

aspects.title: Multi-element region loop: G21 mechanism #1 (Tab must exit the subset after the final location) where no advice is owed
aspects.description: G21's first sufficient mechanism is purely behavioral and needs NO advice: ensure that Tab exits the subset of content after it reaches the final navigation location. The distinguishing failure is a within-region LOOP — focus reaches the last control of a sub-section and Tab wraps back to that section's first control instead of progressing to the rest of the page (Trusted Tester 2.b: access restricted to a small section with no way to navigate out of the loop). The corpus's loops are degenerate — Failed 1/2 self-refocus on ONE element, and the documented-exit ping-pong cases all carry advice or a help link. There is no genuine MULTI-element region loop with NO advice where the only question is the behavioral one: does the final Tab leave the region or wrap? Judging this requires Tabbing to the LAST element of the region and observing whether the next Tab crosses the region boundary — and recognizing that since no escape advice is owed for plain Tab, the page passes iff the loop is broken.
aspects.scLimb: G21 mechanism #1 / TT loop limb: keyboard access not restricted to a small section with no way out of the loop — the pure behavioral question of whether the FINAL Tab exits a multi-element region, no advice owed.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has no substantive multi-element region whose final Tab wraps internally; its loops are single-element self-refocus or are accompanied by documented Ctrl+M advice/help links, so the pure G21-#1 behavioral question (does the LAST Tab exit?) is never isolated. Detecting it requires Tabbing to a region's last control and observing whether the next Tab crosses the region boundary — driving the keyboard, not static analysis.

references.quote: Ensuring that the keyboard function for advancing focus within content (commonly the tab key) exits the subset of the content after it reaches the final navigation location.
Keyboard access is restricted to a small section of the page with no way to navigate out of the "loop" to the rest of the page.

Keyboard focus can be moved away from each section of the page containing elements (not trapped in a "loop" preventing access to other elements) using either standard navigation keys OR documented custom keystrokes.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a substantive page with a real region (carousel, toolbar, card group) of 4-6 focusable controls embedded between page chrome (header nav before, footer links after). FAIL = the region's LAST control has an onkeydown Tab handler that focus()es the region's FIRST control, walling off everything after it, with NO advice. PASS = identical region but the final Tab is left alone so focus flows naturally to the footer links. The only difference must be the last-element Tab behavior; no advice text anywhere, so the judge must rule on behavior alone. Include a Shift-Tab variant (the region's first control's Shift-Tab wraps to the last, walling off content BEFORE the region). Verify a footer 'AFTER' link is or is not reachable.
suggestedScenarios: A 'card carousel' region with five focusable controls where the last control's Tab onkeydown calls focus() on the first control, walling off the page footer links beyond it — a multi-element loop with no advice (FAIL on G21-#1).
The same five-control carousel where the last control's Tab is left alone so focus naturally exits to the footer links (PASS), visually identical to the FAIL variant.
A toolbar region whose FIRST control's Shift-Tab wraps to its own last control, walling off the header navigation BEFORE the region — a reverse-direction loop with no advice (FAIL).
A multi-control 'filters' panel between two content sections where Tab from the last filter returns to the first filter, so the second content section is unreachable by keyboard, no advice (FAIL).
A region of links where Tab exits forward correctly but Shift-Tab from the first link wraps internally — the loop is one-directional, requiring the judge to test BOTH directions (FAIL).

A substantive sidebar widget (5 controls) that loops Tab internally BUT a visible 'Press Ctrl+M to skip this panel' instruction with a working handler is present — PASS via G21 mechanism #2, contrasting the no-advice FAIL to confirm the judge applies the advice clause correctly.

aspects.title: Required-input / sequential-gate exception: a section that demands interaction before focus progresses is NOT a failure
aspects.description: Trusted Tester explicitly carves out a non-failure: if a section of a page requires input or interaction before allowing focus to progress to the rest of the page, this is NOT a keyboard trap failure. The corpus has NO form scenario at all — no <form>, <input>, <select>, or <textarea> anywhere — so this exception is never exercised. The judgment is semantic and easy to get wrong: a required-field gate where focus cannot advance until the user completes the field LOOKS like a trap (Tab does not move focus forward) but is conformant; an actual trap is one where focus cannot advance even AFTER the required interaction is completed, OR where the gate cannot be satisfied by keyboard at all. Distinguishing 'intentional gate the user can satisfy by keyboard' from 'genuine trap' requires understanding the interaction's intent and verifying the gate is keyboard-satisfiable — judgment a tool cannot make.
aspects.scLimb: TT exception limb (Note under Test 2.b): a section requiring input/interaction before allowing focus to progress is NOT a failure — distinguishing a legitimate keyboard-satisfiable gate from a genuine trap.
aspects.whyUncovered: No required-form-field / sequential-gate scenario exists in the corpus (no form, input, select, or textarea anywhere), so the input-gate exception — a section that legitimately holds focus until the user completes an interaction — is never tested. A checker sees 'Tab does not advance' and cannot tell whether the gate is conformant (satisfiable by keyboard) or a trap.

references.quote: *Note:* If a section of a page requires input or interaction before allowing focus to progress to the rest of the page, this is **not** a failure.
Keyboard focus is not considered trapped when the user can navigate away from a component using only a keyboard interface

Keyboard focus can be moved away from each section of the page containing elements (not trapped in a "loop" preventing access to other elements) using either standard navigation keys OR documented custom keystrokes.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build forms/wizards where a step holds focus until a required interaction completes. CONFORMANT PASS = a required field whose validation gate blocks forward Tab while empty, but once the user types a valid value (by keyboard) Tab advances to the rest of the page — focus IS releasable, the hold is intentional. FAIL = a gate that never releases even after the required input is satisfied, OR a gate whose required interaction cannot be performed by keyboard at all (e.g., requires a drag), OR a confirm-checkbox gate where the checkbox is mouse-only. The judge must distinguish 'satisfy-then-advance' (PASS) from 'cannot-advance-ever' or 'cannot-satisfy-by-keyboard' (FAIL). Keep the visual identical so only keyboard interaction resolves it.
suggestedScenarios: A required <input> whose script blocks forward Tab while empty but releases focus to the rest of the form once a valid value is typed by keyboard — a conformant gate that LOOKS like a trap (PASS).
A required field whose Tab-block never releases even after a valid value is entered, so focus can never reach the submit button or beyond — a genuine trap masquerading as a validation gate (FAIL).

A multi-step wizard where Step 1 holds focus until a checkbox is checked, but the checkbox is mouse-only (onclick, not focusable, no keydown) so the gate cannot be satisfied by keyboard at all (FAIL).
A 'I agree to terms' gate that blocks Tab until a checkbox is checked by keyboard (Space), then releases — conformant required interaction (PASS).
A search-as-you-type field that holds focus until at least 3 characters are entered (keyboard-satisfiable) then allows Tab to results — intentional gate, not a trap (PASS).

A field whose forward Tab is blocked by an inline error until the value matches a pattern, but the only way to clear the error is a mouse-driven 'Fix' button — keyboard users can satisfy nothing and never advance (FAIL).

aspects.title: Documented custom-exit advice that is unreachable or inaccurate beyond the corpus's Ctrl+M-before-trap pattern
aspects.description: TT Evaluate-Results 1.b requires custom escape keystrokes to be DOCUMENTED AND AVAILABLE, and How-to-Test 3.a/3.b require checking that contextual help discloses the alternate command and that the command actually works. The corpus covers advice-before-trap, advice-within-trap, and a help-link inside the subset (Passed 4/5/6), plus three failure modes (never advised, generic/non-instructive, named-but-broken). But it tests these only on the Ctrl+M-on-flat-buttons template and only with advice that is either plainly present or plainly absent. The uncovered judgment surface is advice REACHABILITY and ACCURACY in harder forms: advice that exists but is itself only reachable by mouse or after the trap; advice located only in collapsed/off-screen help the keyboard user inside the trap cannot get to; advice that names a key combo with a subtle defect (right key, wrong modifier); or advice that is technically present but describes a DIFFERENT trap. Judging whether documented advice is genuinely AVAILABLE to a trapped keyboard user, and whether it accurately matches the working escape, requires reading intent and driving the keyboard.
aspects.scLimb: Conditional-pass clause: the user IS ADVISED of the method for moving focus away — applied to the REACHABILITY and ACCURACY of the advice (G21: 'document the feature in an accessible manner within the subset'), beyond the corpus's plainly-present/plainly-absent Ctrl+M cases.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT tests advice only as plainly-present (before/within trap, help link) or plainly-absent/generic/named-but-broken, all on the Ctrl+M-flat-button template. It never tests advice that is present but unreachable by a trapped keyboard user, hidden in collapsed/off-screen help, located only AFTER the trap, or accurate-looking but subtly mismatched — the reachability/accuracy judgment G21 demands ('accessible manner within the subset'). A checker cannot judge whether advice is genuinely reachable from inside the trap or whether it matches the real escape.

references.quote: Inspect any contextual/application help and documentation for notification of **available alternate keyboard commands** (non-standard controls, access keys, hotkeys) to escape/avoid the trap.
Custom keystrokes that are **documented and available** to users in the application.
Providing a keyboard function to move the focus out of the subset of the content. Be sure to document the feature in an accessible manner within the subset.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Reuse the documented-custom-exit frame but attack the reachability/accuracy of the advice rather than its bare presence. FAIL variants: the working Ctrl+M exit exists but its only instruction lives in a collapsed <details> or an off-screen 'help' panel the trapped keyboard user cannot open from inside; advice that appears only AFTER the trapped region in DOM/visual order so a trapped user never reaches it; advice as alt text on an image (not read in context) or as a title= tooltip requiring hover; advice naming the right key with a wrong modifier (says 'Ctrl+M' but handler fires on Alt+M); advice that accurately describes a DIFFERENT region's escape. PASS variant: advice reachable by keyboard from within the subset (per Passed 6 help-link pattern) AND matching the working exit. The judge must verify the advice is reachable AND correct, not merely present.
suggestedScenarios: A trap with a working Ctrl+M exit whose only instruction is inside a collapsed <details> located after the trap — a trapped keyboard user can never open it; advice exists but is unavailable (FAIL).

A trap where the escape instruction is present but rendered only as a CSS-offscreen 'skip' hint positioned visually and in DOM AFTER the trapped region, so it is never encountered before being trapped (FAIL).
A trap whose escape advice is the title= tooltip on an icon (revealed on hover only) and is not focusable/announced for keyboard users — advice present but not keyboard-available (FAIL).
A trap whose visible advice reads 'Press Ctrl+M to exit' but the keydown handler fires on Alt+M (right key, wrong modifier) — accurate-looking advice that does not match the working exit (FAIL).

A trap with a help link INSIDE the subset that is keyboard-reachable and reveals 'Press Ctrl+M to exit', and Ctrl+M works — advice both reachable and accurate (PASS, the harder G21 'accessible manner within the subset' case).
A page with two trapping regions where region A's escape advice actually describes region B's keystroke (mismatched), so the advice present in A is inaccurate for A (FAIL).

pages.scenario: SaaS onboarding coachmark embedded as a cross-document <iframe src='case-01-frame.html'>. The embedded mini-app's only control, a 'Got it' button, swallows Tab (keydown preventDefault + self-refocus) and re-grabs focus onblur, so focus enters the iframe and can never cross back to the parent's 'Open dashboard' link. No Esc, no exit advice.
pages.mechanism: F10 cross-document iframe boundary: a capture-phase keydown on Tab inside the embedded document calls preventDefault() and re-focuses the only button, plus a blur->focus() re-grab. The host never receives the boundary-crossing focus event, so a keyboard user cannot return to the parent document. Verified via CDP: 26 Tab presses never reach the AFTER link; Esc does not free focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse parse the host static DOM and see a well-formed iframe with a title and valid src — no missing attribute, empty name, or role error. They do not press Tab, do not model the cross-document focus cycle, and do not follow the embedded document to discover its button cancels Tab. Only driving Tab into the iframe and observing the next Tab never reaches 'Open dashboard' reveals the trap.

citation.quote: Applies when content creates a situation where the user can enter the content using the keyboard, but cannot exit the content using the keyboard.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit donation page with a hosted-card-fields-style payment widget in a cross-document <iframe>. The embedded form re-implements its own tab cycle: the last control ('Donate $25') loops forward Tab back to the first field, and Shift+Tab from the first field loops to the last, so Tab cycles among the widget's controls forever and never crosses the iframe boundary to the parent's 'Cancel and return to home' link. No exit advice.
pages.mechanism: F10 / violation of G21 sufficient mechanism #1: instead of letting Tab exit after the final control, keydown handlers on the first and last embedded controls cancel Tab/Shift+Tab and re-cycle focus within the iframe. The forward-Tab loop at the cross-document boundary is never released. Verified via CDP: 26 Tab presses never leave the iframe; Esc does not free focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Static scanners see a valid iframe with five properly labelled, operable inputs and a named submit button — all name/role/label checks pass. Nothing in the markup declares that forward Tab loops instead of exiting; that is a runtime focus-traversal behavior. Tools never press Tab and never model the cross-document focus cycle, so the boundary loop is invisible. Only tabbing to 'Donate' and finding the next Tab returns to the amount field detects it.

citation.quote: Ensuring that the keyboard function for advancing focus within content (commonly the tab key) exits the subset of the content after it reaches the final navigation location.

pages.scenario: Forum thread reply box implemented as a custom element <comment-composer> whose UI lives in an open Shadow DOM (attachShadow mode:open, delegatesFocus:true). The light-DOM source is just the empty custom-element tag. The component listens for focusout on its shadow root and synchronously re-focuses the textarea, so Tab/Shift+Tab cycle textarea<->button forever and never cross the shadow boundary to the parent's 'Back to all threads' link. No Esc, no advice.
pages.mechanism: F10 applied to a Shadow-DOM boundary: a focusout listener on the shadow root checks whether the new focus target is outside the root and, if so, re-focuses the textarea, preventing focus from ever leaving the shadow tree. The trap is invisible in light-DOM source. Verified via CDP (piercing the open shadow root): 26 Tab presses oscillate only between #ta and #post; the AFTER link is never reached and Esc does not free focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The light-DOM source is a single unknown custom element with no attributes — no role, name, or label to flag. Seeing the textarea/button at all requires instantiating the component and piercing the open shadow root; even then the trap is the focusout re-grab, a runtime behavior. Tools do not run the focus cycle or press Tab, so they cannot observe that focus never leaves the shadow tree.

citation.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that content does not "trap" keyboard focus within subsections of content on a web page. This is a common problem when multiple formats are combined within a page and rendered using plug-ins or embedded applications, or when custom components and widgets are not implemented with keyboard users in mind.

pages.scenario: Knowledge-base Markdown editor as a custom element <markdown-editor> in an open Shadow DOM. Inside the textarea Tab is deliberately captured to insert indentation (the WCAG rich-text-editor example), so plain Tab does not advance focus. BUT a persistent visible instruction inside the shadow root says 'Press Esc to leave the editor', and a working Esc handler blurs the textarea and moves focus across the shadow boundary to the host 'Publish' button. PASS boundary variant.
pages.mechanism: Intentional Tab capture (Tab->indent) rescued by an advised, working non-Tab exit: the Esc keydown handler blurs the textarea and focuses the host's data-after Publish button, crossing the shadow boundary. The SC explicitly allows non-Tab exits when the user is advised and the method works. Verified via CDP: Tab inside the editor keeps focus on the textarea (indent captured); Esc lands focus on the host 'Publish' button (data-after=true).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Structurally indistinguishable from a trapping Shadow-DOM widget (an unknown custom element whose Tab does not advance focus). Whether it is a fatal trap or a legitimate escapable editor depends on three things no scanner can evaluate: that Tab is intentionally captured for indentation, that a visible in-shadow instruction advises Esc, and that the Esc handler genuinely moves focus out across the boundary. Tools never press keys, so they can neither flag a false trap nor certify the real PASS.

citation.quote: If untrapping focus requires a different method (rather than unmodified arrow keys, the Tab key, or other "standard exit methods"), content can still pass this criterion provided that the user is advised how they can untrap focus using their keyboard interface.

pages.scenario: Transit service-update page embeds an interactive route diagram as a separate SVG document via <object type='image/svg+xml' data='case-05-map.svg'>. The SVG's four focusable station <a> links are looped by the SVG's own script (last->first on forward Tab, first->last on Shift+Tab) so Tab never crosses the object boundary to the parent's 'Next: fares & passes' link. A paragraph BEFORE the object reads 'Tab through the diagram, then press Tab once more to continue' — plausible G21-style advice that is in fact FALSE.
pages.mechanism: F10 cross-format (SVG-in-object) trap with present-but-false escape advice: the embedded SVG script cancels forward Tab on the last station and re-focuses the first, cycling within the cross-format document; the printed instruction describes a working exit that does not exist. Per the SC the user must actually be able to untrap focus, and the advised method does not work. Verified via CDP: 26 Tab presses keep focus on the object; the AFTER link is never reached and Esc does not free focus.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A static scan sees a valid object embedding an SVG whose station links carry accessible names, plus a readable paragraph of keyboard instructions — all checks pass. Tools cannot drive Tab into the cross-format SVG document, cannot observe the forward loop, and above all cannot judge that the printed escape advice CONTRADICTS the actual focus behavior. That meaning-vs-behavior comparison (perform the steps, notice the promised exit never happens) is exactly the human reasoning the SC demands.

citation.quote: When content includes multiple formats, one or more user agents or plug-ins are often needed in order to successfully present the content to users. For example, a page that includes HTML, SVG, SMIL and XForms may require a browser to load as many as three different plug-ins in order for a user to successfully interact with the content.

pages.scenario: Podcast episode page embeds an audio-controls panel as a cross-document <iframe>. Inside are real focusable controls (Play/Pause, Rewind, Forward, seek slider, speed select). The player adds legitimate widget behavior (Play toggles label; range uses native arrows) but does NOT intercept Tab anywhere, so forward Tab on the last control falls through and crosses the iframe boundary to the parent's 'Show transcript' link. PASS boundary variant (G21 mechanism #1).
pages.mechanism: G21 sufficient mechanism #1 satisfied: controls are ordinary focusable elements with no Tab interception and no focus re-grab, so after the final control (speed select) a forward Tab advances focus out of the iframe to the host document. Standard Tab exit works, so no documentation is required. Verified via CDP: focus enters the iframe and reaches the AFTER 'Show transcript' link on the 6th Tab press, confirming the boundary is crossed.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: In the DOM this is identical to a trapping iframe: a titled iframe containing several named, operable controls. The only difference is whether the final Tab crosses the boundary, observable solely by pressing Tab through the controls and watching focus land on 'Show transcript'. Tools never press Tab and never model cross-document focus flow, so they can neither detect a trap (there is none) nor certify the no-trap PASS.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal refill modal built with native <dialog open>: a JS focus trap cycles Tab among the refill form's four controls, but there is no Close/Cancel control and no Esc handler. Because the dialog was rendered with the open attribute (not opened via showModal()) the UA's native Esc-cancel is not armed either; only a mouse backdrop-click escapes. Keyboard users are stranded.
pages.mechanism: Focus is restricted to a modal whose cycle contains no keyboard-operable dismiss: the keydown handler early-returns for every key except Tab (so Esc is dead), the dialog has no Close/Cancel to tab to, and <dialog open> (vs showModal()) leaves the UA Esc-cancel inactive. The sole escape is a mouse backdrop mousedown, useless to keyboard/switch/magnifier users.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The DOM is pristine — a genuine <dialog> with UA-inferred modal semantics, aria-labelledby resolving to a real <h2>, a <label> for every field, accessible names everywhere, no contrast issue, nothing missing/empty. axe/WAVE/Lighthouse never press Tab or Esc, so they never observe the cycle has no exit, and they cannot reason about the modal carve-out: the violation is not 'focus cycles' (permissible) but 'no keyboard-operable dismiss exists' — a behavioral + semantic judgment.

citation.quote: There may be times when it's appropriate for a web page to restrict focus to a subsection of the content – for example, when the user is inside a modal dialog or popover. This does not fail the requirements of this criterion, as long as the user knows how to "untrap" the focus and leave that component.

pages.scenario: Government DMV vehicle-registration renewal modal (role=dialog aria-modal=true). Focus IS restricted to the dialog (Tab wraps among its controls), but this is the legitimate-containment carve-out: a wired, functional Esc handler closes the dialog and restores focus to the triggering button, and the focus cycle explicitly includes the focusable header Close (✕) and footer Cancel. The conformant modal the ACT corpus never models.
pages.mechanism: Legitimate focus containment WITH a working keyboard exit: the keydown handler has an Escape branch that calls closeDialog() and restores focus to the opener (lastFocused), and focusables() includes #close-x and #cancel so the wrap cycle reaches a keyboard-operable dismiss. Focus is contained (correct modal behavior per TT 4.C) yet always escapable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A tool can no more confirm this PASS than detect case-01's FAIL: both share the identical static signature (role=dialog, a focus cycle, a Close control in the DOM). Tools never press Esc to verify the exit fires, never Tab the cycle to verify Close is inside it, and cannot reason about the carve-out that makes focus restriction permissible. Certifying the pass and distinguishing it from the visually identical trap requires human keyboard-driving.

citation.quote: A web application opens a dialog box. At the bottom of the dialog are two buttons, "Cancel" and "OK".
